```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)  # linear mixed models with lmer(), used to check the closed form
library(gt)    # nicely formatted tables, not part of the tidyverse

source("../R/simulate_study.R")
source("../R/fit_agreement.R")
source("../R/fit_balanced.R")

# An empty chunk with the same label as a "## ---- label ----" section of the
# simulation script shows that part of the script (appendix E)
knitr::read_chunk("../R/run_simulation.R")

# Results of R/run_simulation.R, one row per simulated dataset
study1 <- read_rds("../results/study1.rds")
study2 <- read_rds("../results/study2.rds")

n_sim <- n_distinct(study1$replicate)  # B
n_boot <- unique(study1$n_boot)        # H
z <- qnorm(0.975)

# The scenarios of R/run_simulation.R, one row each
scenarios_1 <- distinct(study1, block, scenario, icc, n_patients, n_per_patient,
                        true_bias, sd_patient, sd_residual)
scenarios_2 <- distinct(study2, scenario, sd_log_total, icc, n_patients, n_per_patient,
                        true_bias, sd_patient, sd_residual)
V <- mean(scenarios_1$sd_patient^2 + scenarios_1$sd_residual^2)  # 0.74 in every Study 1 scenario

method_colors <- c("Classical" = "#D55E00", "Additive model" = "#009E73",
                   "Multiplicative model" = "#0072B2")
ci_method_colors <- c("Classical, observation bootstrap" = "#D55E00",
                      "Classical, patient bootstrap" = "#E69F00",
                      "Additive model, patient bootstrap" = "#009E73")
percent <- function(x, digits = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f%%"), 100 * x)
```

Two simulation studies from chapter 6 of my thesis.
Each asks what goes wrong when a Bland–Altman analysis ignores the true structure of the data.

- **Study 1. Repeated measurements.** Measurements of the same patient are correlated. What if the analysis treats them as independent?
- **Study 2. Multiplicative error.** The error grows with cardiac output (CO). What if the analysis assumes it is constant?

Both studies follow the same approach.
First derive from the model what should happen, then check it on `r format(n_sim, big.mark = ",")` simulated datasets per scenario.
Three ideas explain every main result, and @fig-theory-vs-simulation shows that the formulas predict the simulation.
All tables and technical details are in the appendix.

```{r}
#| label: measures
#| code-summary: "Code: performance measures and predictions used in every figure"

# ---- Study 1 ----

# True limits of agreement of every scenario
study1 <- study1 |>
  mutate(sd_total = sqrt(sd_patient^2 + sd_residual^2),
         true_lower_loa = true_bias - z * sd_total,
         true_upper_loa = true_bias + z * sd_total)

# Idea 1: predictions for the classical analysis in every scenario
predictions_1 <- scenarios_1 |>
  mutate(design_effect = 1 + (n_per_patient - 1) * icc,
         s2_ratio = 1 - icc * (n_per_patient - 1) / (n_patients * n_per_patient - 1),  # E(s_D^2) / V
         predicted_ratio = sqrt(s2_ratio / design_effect),
         predicted_coverage = 2 * pnorm(z / sqrt(design_effect)) - 1)

# 95% CI for the bias: SE ratio, coverage and width
bias_ci <- study1 |>
  select(block, scenario, icc, n_patients, n_per_patient, true_bias,
         classical_bias, classical_se, additive_bias, additive_se) |>
  pivot_longer(c(classical_bias, classical_se, additive_bias, additive_se),
               names_to = c("method", ".value"), names_pattern = "(classical|additive)_(.*)") |>
  mutate(
    # Classical: IJ independent measurements. Additive model: I independent patients.
    df = if_else(method == "classical", n_patients * n_per_patient - 1, n_patients - 1),
    ci_lower = bias - qt(0.975, df) * se,
    ci_upper = bias + qt(0.975, df) * se,
    covered = ci_lower <= true_bias & true_bias <= ci_upper
  ) |>
  summarize(emp_se = sd(bias),
            model_se = sqrt(mean(se^2)),
            var_se2 = var(se^2),
            coverage = mean(covered),
            width = mean(ci_upper - ci_lower),
            .by = c(block, scenario, icc, n_patients, n_per_patient, method)) |>
  mutate(se_ratio = model_se / emp_se,
         mcse_se_ratio = se_ratio * sqrt(var_se2 / (4 * n_sim * model_se^4) + 1 / (2 * (n_sim - 1))),
         mcse_coverage = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_sim),
         method = factor(method, levels = c("classical", "additive"),
                         labels = c("Classical", "Additive model")))

# Idea 2: SD of an estimated limit, the true one and the one the observation bootstrap sees
sd_limit_true <- function(icc, n_patients, n_per_patient, V) {
  I <- n_patients
  J <- n_per_patient
  var_patient <- icc * V
  var_residual <- (1 - icc) * V
  sqrt(V / (I * J) * (1 + (J - 1) * icc) +
         z^2 * (I * (J - 1) * var_residual^2 + (I - 1) * (J * var_patient + var_residual)^2) / (2 * V * (I * J - 1)^2))
}

sd_limit_observation_bootstrap <- function(n_patients, n_per_patient, V) {
  sqrt(V / (n_patients * n_per_patient) * (1 + z^2 / 2))
}

# Approximate coverage of the observation bootstrap CI of a limit
observation_bootstrap_coverage <- function(icc, n_patients, n_per_patient, V) {
  2 * pnorm(z * sd_limit_observation_bootstrap(n_patients, n_per_patient, V) /
              sd_limit_true(icc, n_patients, n_per_patient, V)) - 1
}

# 95% bootstrap CIs for the limits: coverage and width
loa_coverage <- study1 |>
  select(block, scenario, icc, n_patients, n_per_patient, true_lower_loa, true_upper_loa,
         ends_with(c("_ci_low", "_ci_high"))) |>
  pivot_longer(ends_with(c("_ci_low", "_ci_high")),
               names_to = c("method", "limit", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "(.*)_(lower|upper)_loa_ci_(low|high)") |>
  mutate(truth = if_else(limit == "lower", true_lower_loa, true_upper_loa),
         covered = low <= truth & truth <= high) |>
  summarize(coverage = mean(covered),
            width = mean(high - low),
            .by = c(block, scenario, icc, n_patients, n_per_patient, method, limit)) |>
  mutate(mcse_coverage = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_sim),
         method = factor(method, levels = c("classical_obs", "classical_patient", "additive_patient"),
                         labels = names(ci_method_colors)))

# ---- Study 2 ----

# Idea 3: the constant limits the additive model converges to.
# Reference CO of simulate_study(): log X = a_i + w_ij,
# a_i ~ N(log 5, 0.25^2) for the patient, w_ij ~ N(0, 0.15^2) within the patient.
sd_between <- 0.25
sd_within <- 0.15
mean_x <- 5 * exp((sd_between^2 + sd_within^2) / 2)    # E(X)
mean_x2 <- 25 * exp(2 * (sd_between^2 + sd_within^2))  # E(X^2)
mean_xx <- 25 * exp(2 * sd_between^2 + sd_within^2)    # E(X_ij X_ik), same patient

theory_2 <- scenarios_2 |>
  mutate(var_log = sd_log_total^2,
         mean_q = exp(true_bias + var_log / 2),                  # E(Q)
         mean_q2 = exp(2 * true_bias + 2 * var_log),             # E(Q^2)
         mean_qq = exp(2 * true_bias + var_log + sd_patient^2),  # E(Q_ij Q_ik), same patient
         mu_d = mean_x * (mean_q - 1),
         v_d = mean_x2 * (mean_q2 - 2 * mean_q + 1) - mu_d^2,
         c_d = mean_xx * (mean_qq - 2 * mean_q + 1) - mu_d^2,
         lower_star = mu_d - z * sqrt(v_d),
         upper_star = mu_d + z * sqrt(v_d),
         # CO where each true line crosses the constant limit
         x_lower = lower_star / (exp(true_bias - z * sd_log_total) - 1),
         x_upper = upper_star / (exp(true_bias + z * sd_log_total) - 1))
marked_theory <- filter(theory_2, sd_log_total == 0.20)

# Share of future differences at reference CO x between lower and upper (both in L/min).
# pmax(..., 0): D > -x always, so a lower limit at or below -x is never crossed (log(0) = -Inf).
coverage_at_co <- function(lower, upper, x, log_bias, sd_log) {
  pnorm((log(pmax(1 + upper / x, 0)) - log_bias) / sd_log) -
    pnorm((log(pmax(1 + lower / x, 0)) - log_bias) / sd_log)
}

co_grid <- seq(2, 10, by = 0.25)
study2 <- study2 |>
  mutate(scenario = factor(paste0(scenario, ": SD of log(Y/X) = ", sd_log_total),
                           levels = paste0(scenarios_2$scenario, ": SD of log(Y/X) = ", scenarios_2$sd_log_total)))

# Estimated and true LoA in L/min at each reference CO.
# The multiplicative limits are for log(Y/X): at CO = x they are x * (exp(limit) - 1).
loa_by_co <- study2 |>
  select(scenario, replicate, true_bias, sd_log_total,
         additive_lower_loa, additive_upper_loa, multiplicative_lower_loa, multiplicative_upper_loa) |>
  pivot_longer(c(additive_lower_loa, additive_upper_loa, multiplicative_lower_loa, multiplicative_upper_loa),
               names_to = c("method", "limit"),
               names_pattern = "(additive|multiplicative)_(lower|upper)_loa",
               values_to = "estimate") |>
  cross_join(tibble(co = co_grid)) |>
  mutate(loa = if_else(method == "multiplicative", co * (exp(estimate) - 1), estimate),
         true_log_loa = if_else(limit == "lower", true_bias - z * sd_log_total, true_bias + z * sd_log_total),
         true_loa = co * (exp(true_log_loa) - 1),
         method = factor(method, levels = c("additive", "multiplicative"),
                         labels = c("Additive model", "Multiplicative model")))

loa_band <- loa_by_co |>
  summarize(mean = mean(loa), low = quantile(loa, 0.025), high = quantile(loa, 0.975),
            .by = c(scenario, sd_log_total, method, limit, co))
true_lines <- distinct(loa_by_co, scenario, sd_log_total, limit, co, true_loa)

# Predictive coverage of the estimated limits in every simulated dataset
predictive_2 <- loa_by_co |>
  select(scenario, replicate, method, limit, co, loa, true_bias, sd_log_total) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = limit, values_from = loa) |>
  mutate(coverage = coverage_at_co(lower, upper, co, true_bias, sd_log_total))

predictive_band <- predictive_2 |>
  summarize(mean = mean(coverage), low = quantile(coverage, 0.025), high = quantile(coverage, 0.975),
            .by = c(scenario, sd_log_total, method, co))

# Idea 3: coverage C*(x) of the constant limits L* and U*
theory_curve <- theory_2 |>
  cross_join(tibble(co = co_grid)) |>
  mutate(coverage = coverage_at_co(lower_star, upper_star, co, true_bias, sd_log_total),
         scenario = factor(paste0(scenario, ": SD of log(Y/X) = ", sd_log_total),
                           levels = levels(study2$scenario)))

# ---- Numbers quoted in the text ----
coverage_of <- function(data, ...) filter(data, ...)$coverage
strong <- filter(bias_ci, scenario == "Patient-dominated")
strong_loa <- filter(loa_coverage, scenario == "Patient-dominated", limit == "lower")
marked_coverage <- predictive_2 |>
  filter(sd_log_total == 0.20, co %in% c(3, 8)) |>
  summarize(coverage = mean(coverage), .by = c(method, co))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-theory-vs-simulation
#| fig-cap: "Each point is one scenario, and for idea 3 one scenario at one reference CO from 2 to 10 L/min. Predicted: the formulas of ideas 1 to 3. Simulated: mean over the 1,000 datasets of the scenario. Dashed: predicted = simulated."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
theory_vs_simulation <- bind_rows(
  # Idea 1: CI for the bias, every Study 1 scenario
  bias_ci |>
    left_join(select(predictions_1, scenario, predicted_coverage), by = "scenario") |>
    transmute(idea = "Idea 1: CI for the bias",
              method = as.character(method),
              predicted = if_else(method == "Classical", predicted_coverage, 0.95),
              simulated = coverage),
  # Idea 2: observation bootstrap CI for the lower limit, every Study 1 scenario
  loa_coverage |>
    filter(method == "Classical, observation bootstrap", limit == "lower") |>
    transmute(idea = "Idea 2: CI for the lower LoA",
              method = "Classical",
              predicted = observation_bootstrap_coverage(icc, n_patients, n_per_patient, V),
              simulated = coverage),
  # Idea 3: predictive coverage at each whole CO, both Study 2 scenarios
  predictive_band |>
    filter(co %in% 2:10) |>
    left_join(select(theory_curve, scenario, co, additive_coverage = coverage), by = c("scenario", "co")) |>
    transmute(idea = "Idea 3: predictive coverage at a given CO",
              method = as.character(method),
              predicted = if_else(method == "Additive model", additive_coverage, 0.95),
              simulated = mean)
)

ggplot(theory_vs_simulation, aes(predicted, simulated, color = method, shape = idea)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = method_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0.5, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0.5, 1)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "The formulas predict the simulation",
       x = "Predicted coverage", y = "Simulated coverage", shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

- **Ignoring the patient breaks the uncertainty, not the estimates.** Under strong clustering (ICC = 0.75, 40 patients × 8 measurements), the classical 95% CI for the bias covers the true bias in only `r percent(coverage_of(strong, method == "Classical"), 0)` of the datasets, the additive model in `r percent(coverage_of(strong, method == "Additive model"), 0)`. Both estimate the limits almost without bias.
- **Resampling patients significantly improves the estimation of the uncertainty.** At the same ICC, resampling single measurements covers the lower limit in `r percent(coverage_of(strong_loa, method == "Classical, observation bootstrap"), 0)` of the datasets, resampling patients with the additive model in `r percent(coverage_of(strong_loa, method == "Additive model, patient bootstrap"), 0)`.
- **With multiplicative error, constant limits are wrong at both ends.** The additive limits contain `r percent(coverage_of(marked_coverage, method == "Additive model", co == 3), 0)` of future differences at a CO of 3 L/min and `r percent(coverage_of(marked_coverage, method == "Additive model", co == 8), 0)` at 8 L/min. The multiplicative model contains `r percent(coverage_of(marked_coverage, method == "Multiplicative model", co == 8), 0)` at every CO.

## Study 1: repeated measurements

Each patient is measured $J$ times, and the differences follow the additive model $D_{ij} = \beta_0 + u_i + \varepsilon_{ij}$.
The bias is $\beta_0 = 0.30$ L/min and the total variance is $V = \sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2 = 0.74$, so the true LoA are `r sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", 0.30 - z * sqrt(V), 0.30 + z * sqrt(V))` L/min in every scenario.
What changes is the ICC $\rho = \sigma_u^2/V$, the share of $V$ due to the patient: 0, 0.1, 0.338 and 0.75, with 40 patients × 8 measurements.
The classical analysis treats all $IJ$ differences as independent. The additive model includes the patient effect $u_i$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Why these scenarios"}
Each comparison changes one thing only.

- **$V$ is fixed.** Otherwise a higher ICC would also change the true limits, and a change in coverage could come from the limits, not from the clustering.
- **ICC = 0 is a control.** There the classical analysis is the correct model, so it should do as well as the additive model.
- **A second block keeps $IJ = 160$.** It splits 160 measurements as 20 × 8, 40 × 4 or 80 × 2, at ICC 0.338 and 0.75. The classical analysis sees the same number of measurements in all six designs, and only how they are split between patients changes ([appendix C](#sec-appendix-c)).
:::

### Idea 1: the design effect

The $J$ measurements of a patient share the same $u_i$.
Averaging them removes the residual error but not the patient effect, so they are worth less than $J$ independent measurements, and the mean difference varies more than the classical analysis assumes:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\bar D) = \frac{\sigma_u^2}{I} + \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{IJ} = \frac{V}{IJ}\,\big[1 + (J-1)\rho\big].
$$

The classical analysis estimates this variance by $s_D^2/(IJ) \approx V/(IJ)$ and misses the **design effect** $1 + (J-1)\rho$.
So its 95% CI for the bias covers only about $2\Phi\big(1.96/\sqrt{1 + (J-1)\rho}\big) - 1$ of the time, `r percent(2 * pnorm(z / sqrt(1 + 7 * 0.75)) - 1, 0)` at ICC = 0.75 with $J = 8$.
The additive model uses the SD of the $I$ patient means instead, and its CI is exact at every ICC.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation"}
**The sums of squares.** Everything follows from the patient means $\bar D_i = \beta_0 + u_i + \bar\varepsilon_i$, where $\bar\varepsilon_i$ is the mean of the patient's $J$ residuals.
They are independent and normal with variance $\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2/J$.
The deviations within a patient, $D_{ij} - \bar D_i = \varepsilon_{ij} - \bar\varepsilon_i$, do not contain $u_i$.
So the two sums of squares of the one-way analysis of variance are independent scaled $\chi^2$ variables, and both are independent of $\bar D$:

$$
SS_W = \sum_{i,j}(D_{ij} - \bar D_i)^2 \sim \sigma_\varepsilon^2\,\chi^2_{I(J-1)}, \qquad
SS_B = J\sum_i(\bar D_i - \bar D)^2 \sim \left(J\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2\right)\chi^2_{I-1},
$$

with $J\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2 = V\,[1 + (J-1)\rho]$.

**Variance of the mean.** $\bar D$ is the mean of the $I$ independent patient means, so $\operatorname{Var}(\bar D) = (\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2/J)/I$.
With $\sigma_u^2 = \rho V$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = (1 - \rho)V$ this is $\frac{V}{IJ}\,[J\rho + 1 - \rho]$.

**The classical SE.** The classical variance is $s_D^2 = (SS_W + SS_B)/(IJ - 1)$. With $E(c\,\chi^2_k) = ck$,

$$
E(s_D^2) = \frac{I(J-1)\,\sigma_\varepsilon^2 + (I-1)\left(J\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2\right)}{IJ-1} = V - \frac{(J-1)\,\sigma_u^2}{IJ-1}.
$$

So the mean squared SE that the classical analysis reports is $E(s_D^2)/(IJ)$, while the true variance is $\operatorname{Var}(\bar D)$.
Their ratio gives the predicted SE ratio $\sqrt{E(s_D^2)\,/\,(V[1 + (J-1)\rho])}$ ([appendix C](#sec-appendix-c)).

**The classical coverage.** Replace $s_D^2$ by its mean $\approx V$. Then the classical $t$ statistic is

$$
\frac{\bar D - \beta_0}{s_D/\sqrt{IJ}} \approx \sqrt{1 + (J-1)\rho}\;Z, \qquad Z \sim N(0, 1),
$$

which lies within $\pm 1.96$ with probability $2\Phi\big(1.96/\sqrt{1 + (J-1)\rho}\big) - 1$.
This ignores the sampling variability of $s_D$, so it is an approximation.

**The additive CI is exact.** Its SE is $s_{\bar D}/\sqrt I$, with $s_{\bar D}$ the SD of the $I$ patient means. So

$$
\frac{\bar D - \beta_0}{s_{\bar D}/\sqrt I} \sim t_{I-1}
$$

exactly, because it is the one-sample $t$ statistic of $I$ independent normal patient means.
The squared SE is $s_{\bar D}^2/I = MS_B/(IJ)$ with $MS_B = SS_B/(I - 1)$, so $E(\widehat{SE}^2) = (J\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2)/(IJ) = \operatorname{Var}(\bar D)$, and the SE ratio is 1 up to Monte Carlo error.
When REML is not at the boundary, this is also the model-based variance $\hat\sigma_u^2/I + \hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2/(IJ)$, because $\hat\sigma_u^2 = (MS_B - MS_W)/J$ and $\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = MS_W$ add up to $MS_B/(IJ)$.

**The estimates are fine.** By the formula for $E(s_D^2)$, the classical analysis underestimates $V$ only by the factor $1 - (J-1)\rho/(IJ-1)$, at most `r percent(0.75 * 7 / 319)` here (ICC = 0.75, 40 × 8).
This moves each classical limit inward by only about `r sprintf("%.3f", z * sqrt(V) * (1 - sqrt(1 - 0.75 * 7 / 319)))` L/min, and the effect vanishes as the number of patients grows.
The additive model estimates both variances without bias away from the boundary, because $E(MS_W) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2$ and $E(MS_B - MS_W)/J = \sigma_u^2$.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-bias-coverage
#| fig-cap: "Points: simulated coverage with ±1.96 Monte Carlo SE, 40 patients × 8 measurements. Line: idea 1 for the classical CI, 2Φ(1.96 / √(1 + 7 ICC)) − 1. Dashed: 95%, the exact coverage of the additive CI."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
# Idea 1. Classical CI half-width: 1.96 sqrt(V / IJ). True SE: sqrt(design effect * V / IJ).
classical_theory <- tibble(icc = seq(0, 0.8, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(coverage = 2 * pnorm(z / sqrt(1 + (8 - 1) * icc)) - 1)

bias_ci |>
  filter(block == "ICC") |>
  ggplot(aes(icc, coverage, color = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = classical_theory, aes(icc, coverage), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            color = method_colors["Classical"], alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = coverage - z * mcse_coverage, ymax = coverage + z * mcse_coverage)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = method_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "Ignoring the patient makes the bias CI too narrow",
       x = "ICC (share of the variance of D due to the patient)",
       y = "Coverage of the 95% CI for the bias") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The same formula says how to spend a fixed number of measurements: fewer per patient means a smaller design effect.
With 160 measurements at ICC = 0.75, the classical CI covers `r percent(coverage_of(bias_ci, scenario == "ICC 0.75: 20 patients x 8", method == "Classical"), 0)` of the time with 20 patients × 8 measurements and `r percent(coverage_of(bias_ci, scenario == "ICC 0.75: 80 patients x 2", method == "Classical"), 0)` with 80 × 2 ([appendix C](#sec-appendix-c)).
The estimates themselves are fine. Both methods estimate the limits almost without bias, and their limits contain about 95% of future differences ([appendix C](#sec-appendix-c)).
Ignoring the patient breaks the uncertainty, not the estimates.

### Idea 2: resample the independent unit

The CIs of the limits are percentile bootstrap intervals, in three versions.
The classical limits either resample single measurements (observation bootstrap) or whole patients (patient bootstrap), and the additive limits resample patients.
The two classical versions share the same estimate, so they differ only in what is resampled.

The estimated lower limit is $\hat L = \bar D - 1.96\, s_D$.
Its true variance grows with the ICC through both the mean and the SD:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat L) \approx \frac{V}{IJ}\big[1 + (J-1)\rho\big]
+ 1.96^2\,\frac{I(J-1)\,\sigma_\varepsilon^4 + (I-1)\left(J\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2\right)^2}{2V\,(IJ-1)^2}.
$$

Resampling single measurements treats the $IJ$ differences as independent and sees only $\frac{V}{IJ}\big(1 + 1.96^2/2\big)$, the value at ICC = 0, whatever the ICC.
So its intervals are too short, and more so as the ICC grows. They cover only about $2\Phi(1.96\, SD_{\text{boot}}/SD_{\text{true}}) - 1$ of the time, `r percent(observation_bootstrap_coverage(0.75, 40, 8, V), 0)` at ICC = 0.75 with 40 × 8.
The patient bootstrap resamples the independent units, so it sees both terms.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation"}
**Two sources of variance.** $\bar D$ is independent of $SS_W$ and $SS_B$ (idea 1), so it is independent of $s_D$.
By the delta method, $\operatorname{Var}(s_D) \approx \operatorname{Var}(s_D^2)/(4V)$, and $\operatorname{Var}(s_D^2) = \operatorname{Var}(SS_W + SS_B)/(IJ-1)^2$ with $\operatorname{Var}(c\,\chi^2_k) = 2c^2k$. So

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat L) \approx \underbrace{\frac{V}{IJ}\big[1 + (J-1)\rho\big]}_{\text{from } \bar D}
+ 1.96^2\,\underbrace{\frac{I(J-1)\,\sigma_\varepsilon^4 + (I-1)\left(J\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2\right)^2}{2V\,(IJ-1)^2}}_{\text{from } s_D}.
$$

The first term is the design effect of idea 1.
In the second, with strong clustering $s_D^2$ is driven by $SS_B$, which has $I - 1$ degrees of freedom, not $IJ - 1$.

**What the observation bootstrap sees.** The resampled mean has variance about $s_D^2/(IJ) \approx V/(IJ)$.
Each $D_{ij}$ is marginally $N(\beta_0, V)$, so the pooled differences have a fourth central moment of about $3V^2$, and the resampled SD has variance about $(3V^2 - V^2)/(4V \cdot IJ) = V/(2IJ)$.
The two are nearly uncorrelated because the distribution is symmetric.
At ICC = 0 the two variances agree, so the predicted coverage is 95% there.

**Coverage.** With $SD_{\text{true}}$ and $SD_{\text{boot}}$ the square roots of the two variances, the observation bootstrap CI is about $1.96\, SD_{\text{boot}}$ wide on each side of the estimate, while the estimate varies with SD $SD_{\text{true}}$. So it covers the true limit with probability about $2\Phi(1.96\, SD_{\text{boot}}/SD_{\text{true}}) - 1$.
:::

What a 95% CI promises is easiest to see one dataset at a time.
Each horizontal line below is the CI from one simulated dataset, and the dot is that dataset's estimate of the lower limit.
A 95% procedure should reach the true limit (dashed) in about 95 of every 100 datasets.

```{r}
#| label: fig-loa-intervals
#| fig-cap: "95% CIs of the lower LoA in 100 randomly chosen simulated datasets (the same datasets in every panel), ordered by the estimate, 40 patients × 8 measurements. Dashed: true lower LoA. Black: the CI misses it. The coverage in each panel is over all 1,000 datasets."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 9
set.seed(3)
shown <- sample(n_sim, 100)  # the same 100 datasets in every panel
true_lower <- 0.30 - z * sqrt(V)

intervals <- study1 |>
  filter(block == "ICC", icc %in% c(0, 0.75), replicate %in% shown) |>
  select(icc, replicate, classical_lower_loa, additive_lower_loa, matches("lower_loa_ci_(low|high)$")) |>
  pivot_longer(matches("lower_loa_ci_(low|high)$"),
               names_to = c("method", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "(.*)_lower_loa_ci_(low|high)") |>
  mutate(estimate = if_else(method == "additive_patient", additive_lower_loa, classical_lower_loa),
         result = if_else(low <= true_lower & true_lower <= high, "Contains the true limit", "Misses it"),
         method = factor(method, levels = c("classical_obs", "classical_patient", "additive_patient"),
                         labels = names(ci_method_colors))) |>
  mutate(rank = rank(estimate, ties.method = "first"), .by = c(icc, method))

panel_labels <- loa_coverage |>
  filter(block == "ICC", icc %in% c(0, 0.75), limit == "lower") |>
  mutate(label = paste("Coverage:", percent(coverage)))

ggplot(intervals, aes(y = rank)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high, color = result)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = estimate, color = result), size = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_lower, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(data = panel_labels, aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
            hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.5, size = 3.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(method ~ icc, labeller = labeller(icc = as_labeller(\(x) paste("ICC =", x)),
                                               method = label_wrap_gen(20))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Contains the true limit" = "grey70", "Misses it" = "black"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = c(1, 12))) +
  labs(title = "Resampling measurements gives intervals too short to reach the truth",
       x = "Lower LoA (L/min): estimate and 95% CI", y = "100 simulated datasets, ordered by the estimate") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
```

At ICC = 0 the three procedures look alike and about 5 lines in 100 miss.
At ICC = 0.75 the estimates spread much more, but the observation bootstrap intervals stay as short as at ICC = 0, so many miss.
The width of the intervals shows it directly: a calibrated 95% CI needs a width of about $2 \times 1.96 \times SD_{\text{true}}$, which grows with the ICC.

```{r}
#| label: fig-loa-width
#| fig-cap: "Each violin and box shows how wide the 95% CIs of the lower LoA were in the 1,000 simulated datasets (40 patients × 8 measurements). Black bar: the width a CI needs to contain the true limit in 95% of the datasets, 2 × 1.96 × the SD of the estimated limit between datasets. Dotted line: the width that idea 2 predicts for the observation bootstrap, the same at every ICC. A box below its black bar means intervals that are too short, so they miss the true limit more than 5% of the time. The upper LoA looks the same."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
widths <- study1 |>
  filter(block == "ICC") |>
  select(icc, replicate, matches("lower_loa_ci_(low|high)$")) |>
  pivot_longer(matches("lower_loa_ci_(low|high)$"),
               names_to = c("method", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "(.*)_lower_loa_ci_(low|high)") |>
  mutate(width = high - low,
         method = factor(method, levels = c("classical_obs", "classical_patient", "additive_patient"),
                         labels = names(ci_method_colors)))

# Idea 2
needed_width <- tibble(icc = unique(widths$icc)) |>
  mutate(width = 2 * z * sd_limit_true(icc, n_patients = 40, n_per_patient = 8, V = V))
observation_width <- 2 * z * sd_limit_observation_bootstrap(n_patients = 40, n_per_patient = 8, V = V)

ggplot(widths, aes(factor(icc), width, fill = method)) +
  geom_violin(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), scale = "width", alpha = 0.3, color = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.15, alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_errorbar(data = needed_width, aes(factor(icc), ymin = width, ymax = width),
                inherit.aes = FALSE, width = 0.9, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = observation_width, linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ci_method_colors, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The observation bootstrap does not widen its CIs as the ICC grows",
       x = "ICC", y = "Width of the 95% CI of the lower LoA (L/min)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")
```

As predicted, the observation bootstrap gives about `r sprintf("%.2f", observation_width)` L/min at every ICC, while a calibrated CI must grow to `r sprintf("%.2f", needed_width$width[needed_width$icc == 0.75])` L/min at ICC = 0.75.
The patient bootstrap intervals grow with the ICC but stay a little short of the black bars, which is why their coverage is a few points below 95% ([appendix C](#sec-appendix-c)).

## Study 2: multiplicative error

Now the error is proportional to the CO: $\log(Y_{ij}/X_{ij}) = \beta_0 + u_i + \varepsilon_{ij}$, with a geometric mean ratio $e^{\beta_0} = 1.05$, a log-scale ICC of 0.338 and an SD $\sigma = 0.20$ of $\log(Y/X)$, for 40 patients × 8 measurements.
The reference $X$ is log-normal around 5 L/min.
Both models include the patient. The multiplicative model is fitted to $\log(Y/X)$, the additive model to $Y - X$ in L/min.
[Appendix D](#sec-appendix-d) adds a milder scenario with $\sigma = 0.10$, which looks the same with smaller effects.

### Idea 3: constant limits cannot follow an error that grows with CO

With $Q = Y/X$, the difference is $D = X(Q - 1)$. So at a reference CO $x$ the true limits are two lines through the origin:

$$
L(x) = x\left(e^{\beta_0 - 1.96\sigma} - 1\right), \qquad U(x) = x\left(e^{\beta_0 + 1.96\sigma} - 1\right).
$$

The multiplicative model estimates these lines, so it has the same coverage at every CO.
The additive model converges to one constant pair of limits $[L^*, U^*] = \mu_D \mp 1.96\sqrt{V_D}$, with $\mu_D$ and $V_D$ the mean and variance of $D$ over all CO.
Each constant limit is right at one CO only: the upper at $x_U$ = `r sprintf("%.1f", marked_theory$x_upper)` L/min and the lower at $x_L$ = `r sprintf("%.1f", marked_theory$x_lower)` L/min.
Below these CO the constant limits are too wide, above them too narrow, and the share of future differences between them falls from 1 to 0 as the CO grows:

$$
C^*(x) = \Phi\left(\frac{\log(1 + U^*/x) - \beta_0}{\sigma}\right) - \Phi\left(\frac{\log(1 + L^*/x) - \beta_0}{\sigma}\right).
$$

This error is a bias, not noise, so more patients do not fix it: the additive limits converge to $L^*$ and $U^*$, which match the true lines only at $x_U$ and $x_L$.
The constant limits also depend on who was studied, not only on the device.
If every reference CO were multiplied by $\lambda$, every difference would be too, so $L^*$, $U^*$, $x_U$ and $x_L$ would all scale by $\lambda$.
The same device would get additive limits half as wide in a population with half the CO, again right only near that population's typical CO.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation"}
**The true limits.** Write $Q = Y/X$, so $\log Q \sim N(\beta_0, \sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2 = \sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2$. In the simulation, $Q$ is independent of $X$.
Given $X = x$, the difference $d = x(Q - 1)$ is increasing in $Q$, so its 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles are $L(x)$ and $U(x)$.
At CO $x$, the estimated lines of the multiplicative model are $x(\hat L_{\text{ratio}} - 1)$ and $x(\hat U_{\text{ratio}} - 1)$, and a future difference is $x(Q - 1)$. Dividing by $x > 0$, the difference is between the lines exactly when $Q$ is between $\hat L_{\text{ratio}}$ and $\hat U_{\text{ratio}}$. This does not depend on $x$, so the multiplicative model has the same coverage at every CO.
These statements are conditional on $X = x$, so they do not depend on the distribution of $X$.

**What the additive model converges to.** In a balanced design its estimates are

$$
\hat\beta_0 = \bar D, \qquad
\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = MS_W, \qquad
\hat\sigma_u^2 = \frac{MS_B - MS_W}{J}, \qquad
[\hat L, \hat U] = \hat\beta_0 \mp 1.96\sqrt{\hat\sigma_u^2 + \hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2}.
$$

The differences of one patient are exchangeable:

$$
E(D_{ij}) = \mu_D, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}(D_{ij}) = V_D, \qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(D_{ij}, D_{ik}) = c_D \quad (j \ne k).
$$

So, whatever their distribution,

$$
E(MS_W) = \frac{1}{J-1}\,E\sum_{j}\left(D_{ij} - \bar D_i\right)^2 = V_D - c_D, \qquad
E(MS_B) = J \operatorname{Var}(\bar D_i) = V_D + (J - 1)\,c_D,
$$

and by the law of large numbers, as $I \to \infty$,

$$
\hat\beta_0 \xrightarrow{\;p\;} \mu_D, \qquad
\hat\sigma_u^2 \xrightarrow{\;p\;} c_D, \qquad
\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \xrightarrow{\;p\;} V_D - c_D, \qquad
[\hat L, \hat U] \xrightarrow{\;p\;} [L^*, U^*] = \mu_D \mp 1.96\sqrt{V_D}.
$$

Because $X$ and $Q$ are independent, each moment splits into a product:

$$
\mu_D = E(X)\,[E(Q) - 1], \qquad
V_D = E(X^2)\,E[(Q - 1)^2] - \mu_D^2, \qquad
c_D = E(X_{ij}X_{ik})\,E[(Q_{ij} - 1)(Q_{ik} - 1)] - \mu_D^2.
$$

All of them are log-normal moments, $E(e^W) = e^{m + s^2/2}$ for $W \sim N(m, s^2)$.
In `simulate_study()` the reference CO is $\log X_{ij} = a_i + w_{ij}$, with the patient's level $a_i \sim N(\log 5, s_b^2)$ and a change within the patient $w_{ij} \sim N(0, s_w^2)$, $s_b = 0.25$ and $s_w = 0.15$. So

- $E(Q) = e^{\beta_0 + \sigma^2/2}$, $E(Q^2) = e^{2\beta_0 + 2\sigma^2}$ and $E(Q_{ij}Q_{ik}) = e^{2\beta_0 + \sigma^2 + \sigma_u^2}$ for $j \ne k$, because $\log Q_{ij} + \log Q_{ik} = 2\beta_0 + 2u_i + \varepsilon_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ik}$ has variance $4\sigma_u^2 + 2\sigma_\varepsilon^2$.
- $E(X) = 5\,e^{(s_b^2 + s_w^2)/2}$, $E(X^2) = 25\,e^{2(s_b^2 + s_w^2)}$ and $E(X_{ij}X_{ik}) = 25\,e^{2s_b^2 + s_w^2}$ for $j \ne k$.

Two measurements of the same patient share $a_i$, so $E(X_{ij}X_{ik}) = E(X)^2 e^{s_b^2}$ is larger than $E(X)^2$.
So part of the patient variance $c_D$ of the additive model only says that patients have different CO levels, not that the device behaves differently in them.
With an independent $X$ for every measurement, as in my thesis, this part would vanish.
[Appendix D](#sec-appendix-d) compares $\mu_D$, $c_D$, $V_D$, $L^*$ and $U^*$ with the simulation.

**The limits depend on the study population.** Replace every reference CO $X$ by $\lambda X$, with $\lambda > 0$ and the same $Q$.
Every difference $D = X(Q - 1)$ becomes $\lambda D$, so

$$
\mu_D \to \lambda\,\mu_D, \qquad V_D \to \lambda^2 V_D, \qquad c_D \to \lambda^2 c_D, \qquad [L^*, U^*] \to [\lambda L^*, \lambda U^*].
$$

The moment formulas above give the same result, because $X$ enters them only through $E(X)$, $E(X^2)$ and $E(X_{ij}X_{ik})$, which scale by $\lambda$, $\lambda^2$ and $\lambda^2$.
In `simulate_study()` this is a population with median CO $5\lambda$ instead of 5 L/min.
The true lines $L(x)$ and $U(x)$ do not change, because they depend only on $Q$.

**Where each constant limit is right.** The true lower line crosses $L^*$ at $x_L = L^*/(e^{\beta_0 - 1.96\sigma} - 1)$, and the upper line crosses $U^*$ at $x_U = U^*/(e^{\beta_0 + 1.96\sigma} - 1)$.
Below these CO the constant limits are too wide, above them too narrow.
So the CIs of the additive limits can only cover the true limits near $x_L$ and $x_U$.
$L^*$ and $U^*$ are limits as $I \to \infty$, so this error does not shrink with more patients: at every other CO the additive limits converge to the wrong value, and their CIs shrink around it.
Since $x_L$ and $x_U$ are proportional to $L^*$ and $U^*$, they also scale by $\lambda$. Whatever the population, the constant limits are right only near its own typical CO.

**Coverage at CO $x$.** A future difference at $X = x$ is between constant limits $L$ and $U$ if and only if $\log(1 + L/x) \le \log Q \le \log(1 + U/x)$, which gives the formula for $C(x)$.
Its second term is 0 when $1 + L/x \le 0$, because $Y > 0$ means $D > -x$.
For $L < 0 < U$, the upper bound decreases and the lower bound increases with $x$, so $C(x)$ decreases strictly, from 1 as $x \to 0$ to 0 as $x \to \infty$.
With $L^*$ and $U^*$, $C^*(x)$ therefore reaches 95% at one CO only, between $x_U$ and $x_L$.
In a population scaled by $\lambda$ the limits are $\lambda L^*$ and $\lambda U^*$, and since $C$ depends on them only through $L/x$ and $U/x$, the coverage becomes $C^*(x/\lambda)$: the same curve, stretched along the CO axis.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="The same limits on a Bland–Altman plot against the mean"}
The figures here plot the difference against the reference $X$. A Bland–Altman plot usually puts the pairwise mean $M = (X + Y)/2$ on the horizontal axis instead.
With $Y = XQ$ the mean is $M = X(1 + Q)/2$, so $X = 2M/(1 + Q)$, and a ratio $q$ corresponds to the difference

$$
d(m, q) = \frac{2m(q - 1)}{q + 1} = 2m \tanh\left(\frac{\log q}{2}\right)
$$

at mean $m$. It is increasing in $q$, so with the ratio limits $L_{\text{ratio}} = e^{\beta_0 - 1.96\sigma}$ and $U_{\text{ratio}} = e^{\beta_0 + 1.96\sigma}$ the limits on the Bland–Altman plot are again two lines through the origin [@parner2025]:

$$
L(m) = \frac{2m\left(L_{\text{ratio}} - 1\right)}{L_{\text{ratio}} + 1} = 2m\tanh\left(\frac{\beta_0 - 1.96\sigma}{2}\right), \qquad
U(m) = \frac{2m\left(U_{\text{ratio}} - 1\right)}{U_{\text{ratio}} + 1} = 2m\tanh\left(\frac{\beta_0 + 1.96\sigma}{2}\right).
$$

A pair lies between the two lines exactly when its ratio $Q$ lies between the ratio limits, so the band contains 95% of all pairs.
Unlike $L(x)$ and $U(x)$, these are not limits for a fixed mean $m$, because $M$ itself depends on $Q$.

**Their width.** I found no published derivation of the width, so I derived it in my thesis:

$$
W(m) = U(m) - L(m) = \frac{4m\left(U_{\text{ratio}} - L_{\text{ratio}}\right)}{\left(1 + U_{\text{ratio}}\right)\left(1 + L_{\text{ratio}}\right)}
= \frac{4m\sinh(1.96\sigma)}{\cosh\beta_0 + \cosh(1.96\sigma)}.
$$

For the last step, write $a = (\beta_0 + 1.96\sigma)/2$ and $b = (\beta_0 - 1.96\sigma)/2$.
Then $\tanh a - \tanh b = \sinh(a - b)/(\cosh a \cosh b)$ and $2\cosh a\cosh b = \cosh(a + b) + \cosh(a - b) = \cosh\beta_0 + \cosh(1.96\sigma)$.
Without multiplicative bias, $\beta_0 = 0$, it reduces to $W(m) = 4m\tanh(0.98\sigma)$.
Against the reference the width is $W(x) = x\left(U_{\text{ratio}} - L_{\text{ratio}}\right) = 2x\,e^{\beta_0}\sinh(1.96\sigma)$.
Both widths grow linearly, in $m$ and in $x$.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-loa-by-co
#| fig-cap: "SD of log(Y/X) = 0.20. Lines: mean estimated limits of agreement over the simulated datasets. Bands: 2.5% to 97.5% of the datasets. Dashed: true limits. Points: the CO where each constant additive limit is right (idea 3)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
crossings <- tibble(co = c(marked_theory$x_upper, marked_theory$x_lower),
                    loa = c(marked_theory$upper_star, marked_theory$lower_star),
                    label = c("x[U]", "x[L]"))

ggplot(filter(loa_band, sd_log_total == 0.20),
       aes(co, mean, color = method, fill = method, group = interaction(method, limit))) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_line(data = filter(true_lines, sd_log_total == 0.20), aes(co, true_loa, group = limit),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = crossings, aes(co, loa), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = crossings, aes(co, loa, label = label), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            parse = TRUE, vjust = -0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = method_colors, name = NULL, aesthetics = c("color", "fill")) +
  labs(title = "Constant limits cannot follow an error that grows with CO",
       x = "Reference CO X (L/min)", y = "Limits of agreement for Y - X (L/min)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-predictive-study2
#| fig-cap: "SD of log(Y/X) = 0.20. Lines: mean predictive coverage over the simulated datasets. Bands: 2.5% to 97.5% of the datasets, not a confidence interval. Dotted: C*(x) from idea 3. Dashed: 95%."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(filter(predictive_band, sd_log_total == 0.20), aes(co, mean, color = method, fill = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_line(data = filter(theory_curve, sd_log_total == 0.20), aes(co, coverage),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "black", linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_color_manual(values = method_colors, name = NULL, aesthetics = c("color", "fill")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "Additive limits: too wide at low CO, too narrow at high CO",
       x = "Reference CO X (L/min)", y = "Predictive coverage") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The additive model follows $C^*(x)$ closely, slightly below it because its limits are estimated, and contains 95% of future differences only between $x_U$ and $x_L$.
For the same reason, its CIs can only cover the true limits near $x_U$ and $x_L$ ([appendix D](#sec-appendix-d)).

## Appendix

### A. Monte Carlo framework

Each scenario has $B$ = `r format(n_sim, big.mark = ",")` simulated datasets.
In dataset $b$, a method gives an estimate $\hat\theta_b$ of a true value $\theta$, for example the lower LoA. Some metrics also use its standard error $\widehat{SE}_b$ or its 95% CI $[c_b^-, c_b^+]$.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false" title="How to read the table"}
Metric
:   what we measure.

Estimate
:   how we compute it from the $B$ datasets.

Monte Carlo SE
:   how precise that estimate is.

Interpretation
:   the question the metric answers.
:::

| Metric | Estimate | Monte Carlo SE | Interpretation |
|---|---|---| --- |
| Bias | $\bar{\hat\theta} - \theta$, with $\bar{\hat\theta} = \frac1B\sum_b \hat\theta_b$ | $SE_{\text{emp}}/\sqrt B$ | Is the method right on average? |
| Empirical SE | $SE_{\text{emp}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_b (\hat\theta_b - \bar{\hat\theta})^2}$ | $SE_{\text{emp}}/\sqrt{2(B-1)}$ | How variable are the estimates between datasets? |
| Model SE / empirical SE | $R = SE_{\text{mod}}/SE_{\text{emp}}$, with $SE_{\text{mod}} = \sqrt{\frac1B\sum_b \widehat{SE}_b^2}$ | $R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{SE}_b^2)}{4B\,SE_{\text{mod}}^4} + \frac{1}{2(B-1)}}$ | Does the method report the right uncertainty? |
| CI coverage | $\hat p = \frac1B\sum_b \mathbb 1\{c_b^- \le \theta \le c_b^+\}$ | $\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/B}$ | How often does the CI contain the true value? |
| CI width | $\frac1B\sum_b (c_b^+ - c_b^-)$ | $SD(c_b^+ - c_b^-)/\sqrt B$ | How wide are the CIs? |
| Predictive coverage | $\frac1B\sum_b p_b$, see below | $SD(p_b)/\sqrt B$ | How often do future differences fall between the estimated limits? |

- $R < 1$ means that the reported SE is too small, so the CIs are too narrow.
- Coverage and width go together: any interval reaches 95% if it is wide enough.
- The Monte Carlo SE is the simulation error of each metric. It shrinks with $B$, not with the sample size of the study.

With $B = 1{,}000$, a coverage near 95% has a Monte Carlo SE of $\sqrt{0.95 \cdot 0.05 / 1000} \approx 0.7 \%$.
The CIs of the LoA are percentile intervals from $H$ = `r n_boot` bootstrap replicates within each dataset.
A larger $H$ makes each interval less noisy, but it does not reduce the Monte Carlo SE, which depends on $B$.

**Predictive coverage** is a different question.
CI coverage asks whether the CI of a limit contains the true limit.
Predictive coverage asks what share of future differences, from new patients, falls between the estimated limits $\hat L_b$ and $\hat U_b$.
It is computed exactly from the true distribution of $D$, not by simulating new patients.

### B. Fast fitting: closed-form REML

`lmer()` needs about 12 ms per fit, far too slow for `r format(n_sim, big.mark = ",")` datasets times `r n_boot` bootstrap refits.
But every design here is balanced, and then REML for the random-intercept model has a closed form.
With patient means $\bar D_i$, grand mean $\bar D$, $MS_W = \frac{1}{I(J-1)}\sum_{i,j}(D_{ij} - \bar D_i)^2$ and $MS_B = \frac{J}{I-1}\sum_i (\bar D_i - \bar D)^2$,

$$
\hat\beta_0 = \bar D, \qquad
\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = MS_W, \qquad
\hat\sigma_u^2 = \frac{MS_B - MS_W}{J}, \qquad
\widehat{SE}(\hat\beta_0) = \sqrt{\frac{MS_B}{IJ}} = \frac{s_{\bar D}}{\sqrt I}.
$$

If $MS_B < MS_W$, this $\hat\sigma_u^2$ would be negative.
REML then puts it on the boundary, $\hat\sigma_u^2 = 0$, and re-estimates $\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = SS_T/(IJ - 1)$ from all differences.
For the bootstrap, the mean and the within-patient sum of squares of each patient are computed once, so each bootstrap replicate only resamples $I$ pairs of numbers (`R/fit_balanced.R`).

The table compares the closed form with `fit_agreement()`, which uses `lmer()`, on three datasets.
The last one has no patient effect and hits the boundary.

```{r}
#| label: closed-form-check
#| message: false
# Additive model fitted to the same data with the closed form and with lmer()
compare_fits <- function(icc, seed, dataset) {
  data <- simulate_study(scale = "additive", sd_patient = sqrt(icc * V),
                         sd_residual = sqrt((1 - icc) * V), seed = seed)
  n_patients <- n_distinct(data$patient)
  t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = n_patients - 1)

  d <- matrix(data$difference, nrow = n_patients, byrow = TRUE)
  closed_form <- fit_balanced(d) |>
    mutate(bias_lower = bias - t_crit * se,
           bias_upper = bias + t_crit * se)
  with_lmer <- fit_agreement(data, response = "difference")

  quantities <- c(bias = "Bias", bias_lower = "Bias CI, lower end", bias_upper = "Bias CI, upper end",
                  sd_patient = "SD between patients", sd_residual = "SD within patient",
                  lower_loa = "Lower LoA", upper_loa = "Upper LoA")
  tibble(dataset = dataset,
         quantity = unname(quantities),
         closed_form = unname(unlist(closed_form[names(quantities)])),
         lmer = unname(unlist(with_lmer[names(quantities)])))
}

validation <- bind_rows(
  compare_fits(icc = 0.750, seed = 1, dataset = "ICC 0.75"),
  compare_fits(icc = 0.338, seed = 1, dataset = "ICC 0.338"),
  compare_fits(icc = 0, seed = 1, dataset = "ICC 0 (boundary: sigma_u = 0)")
) |>
  mutate(difference = abs(closed_form - lmer))

validation |>
  gt(groupname_col = "dataset") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(closed_form, lmer), decimals = 4) |>
  fmt_scientific(columns = difference, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_header(title = "Closed form vs lmer()", subtitle = "40 patients x 8 measurements") |>
  cols_label(quantity = "", closed_form = "Closed form", lmer = "lmer()", difference = "Difference")
```

All estimates agree up to the tolerance of the `lmer()` optimizer.
The only difference is the bias CI at the boundary.
There `lmer()` computes the SE from the re-estimated $\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2$, while the closed form keeps the SD of the patient means, as in the thesis.
With it, the $t$ interval is exact in every dataset, because the $I$ patient means are independent and normal.
At ICC = 0, `r percent(mean(study1$additive_boundary[study1$icc == 0]), 0)` of the simulated datasets hit the boundary.

### C. Study 1 in full {#sec-appendix-c}

**The two analyses.** In a balanced design both use the mean of all differences as the bias.
They differ in the SE of the bias and in the SD used for the limits.

| | Classical | Additive model |
|---|---|---|
| SD for the LoA | $s_D$, SD of all $IJ$ differences | $\sqrt{\hat\sigma_u^2 + \hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2}$ (REML) |
| SE of the bias | $s_D/\sqrt{IJ}$ | $s_{\bar D}/\sqrt I$, with $s_{\bar D}$ the SD of the $I$ patient means |
| 95% CI for the bias | $\bar D \pm t_{0.975,\,IJ-1}\, SE$ | $\bar D \pm t_{0.975,\,I-1}\, SE$ |

**Scenarios and predictions.** Idea 1 for the classical analysis in every scenario. For the additive model, idea 1 predicts an SE ratio of 1 and a coverage of 95% everywhere.

```{r}
#| label: study1-predictions
predictions_1 |>
  select(block, scenario, icc, n_patients, n_per_patient, design_effect, s2_ratio,
         predicted_ratio, predicted_coverage) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "block") |>
  fmt_number(columns = icc, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(design_effect, s2_ratio, predicted_ratio), decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = predicted_coverage, decimals = 0) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Classical analysis, predicted", columns = c(s2_ratio, predicted_ratio, predicted_coverage)) |>
  tab_header(title = "Study 1 scenarios and the predictions for the classical analysis",
             subtitle = "ICC block: 40 x 8 = 320 measurements. Allocation block: 160 measurements.") |>
  cols_label(scenario = "", icc = "ICC", n_patients = "Patients I",
             n_per_patient = "Measurements per patient J", design_effect = "Design effect",
             s2_ratio = html("E(s<sub>D</sub><sup>2</sup>) / V"), predicted_ratio = "SE ratio",
             predicted_coverage = "Bias CI coverage")
```

**Allocation of 160 measurements.**

```{r}
#| label: fig-bias-coverage-allocation

ggplot(allocation, aes(design, coverage, color = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed") +

       x = "Patients x measurements per patient", y = "Coverage of the 95% CI for the bias") +
  theme_minimal() +

```

**Point estimates.**

```{r}
#| label: study1-point
study1 |>
  filter(block == "ICC") |>
  select(icc, true_lower_loa, true_upper_loa,
         classical_lower_loa, classical_upper_loa, additive_lower_loa, additive_upper_loa) |>
  pivot_longer(c(classical_lower_loa, classical_upper_loa, additive_lower_loa, additive_upper_loa),
               names_to = c("method", "limit"), names_pattern = "(classical|additive)_(.*)",
               values_to = "estimate") |>
  mutate(truth = if_else(limit == "lower_loa", true_lower_loa, true_upper_loa)) |>
  summarize(bias = mean(estimate - truth),
            emp_se = sd(estimate),
            .by = c(icc, method, limit)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = limit, values_from = c(bias, emp_se)) |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = c("classical", "additive"),
                         labels = c("Classical", "Additive model"))) |>
  arrange(icc, method) |>
  select(icc, method, bias_lower_loa, emp_se_lower_loa, bias_upper_loa, emp_se_upper_loa) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = -method, decimals = 3) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Lower LoA", columns = ends_with("lower_loa")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Upper LoA", columns = ends_with("upper_loa")) |>
  tab_header(title = "Both methods estimate the limits well",
             subtitle = "Bias and empirical SE of the estimated LoA in L/min, 40 patients x 8 measurements") |>
  tab_source_note("Bias = mean estimate - true value. Its Monte Carlo SE is the empirical SE / sqrt(B).") |>
  cols_label(icc = "ICC", method = "", bias_lower_loa = "Bias", emp_se_lower_loa = "Empirical SE",
             bias_upper_loa = "Bias", emp_se_upper_loa = "Empirical SE")
```

As idea 1 says, both methods estimate the limits almost without bias.
The bias estimate is the same for both in a balanced design.
The classical limits are slightly too narrow at high ICC, because $E(s_D^2) < V$, but the effect is small compared with the empirical SE.

**Confidence interval for the bias.**

```{r}
#| label: study1-bias-table
bias_ci |>
  left_join(select(predictions_1, scenario, predicted_ratio, predicted_coverage), by = "scenario") |>
  # Idea 1: the additive model has SE ratio 1 and coverage 95% in every scenario
  mutate(predicted_ratio = if_else(method == "Classical", predicted_ratio, 1),
         predicted_coverage = if_else(method == "Classical", predicted_coverage, 0.95)) |>
  arrange(block != "ICC", icc, n_per_patient, method) |>
  select(scenario, method, emp_se, model_se, predicted_ratio, se_ratio, predicted_coverage, coverage, width) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "scenario") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(emp_se, model_se, predicted_ratio, se_ratio, width), decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(predicted_coverage, coverage), decimals = 1) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "SE ratio", columns = c(predicted_ratio, se_ratio)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Coverage", columns = c(predicted_coverage, coverage)) |>
  tab_header(title = "Bias CI: the classical SE ignores the design effect",
             subtitle = "SE ratio = model SE / empirical SE. Predicted: idea 1. Width in L/min.") |>
  tab_source_note(sprintf("Largest Monte Carlo SE: %.3f for the ratio, %.1f percentage points for the coverage.",
                          max(bias_ci$mcse_se_ratio), 100 * max(bias_ci$mcse_coverage))) |>
  cols_label(method = "", emp_se = "Empirical SE", model_se = "Model SE",
             predicted_ratio = "Predicted", se_ratio = "Simulated",
             predicted_coverage = "Predicted", coverage = "Simulated", width = "Width")
```

The simulated SE ratios match idea 1 within Monte Carlo error.
So the classical CI misses more often as the ICC and the number of measurements per patient grow, while the additive model stays at 95% in every scenario.
The classical coverage is within 3 points of its approximate prediction, which ignores the sampling variability of $s_D$.

**Confidence intervals for the limits of agreement.**

```{r}
#| label: fig-loa-coverage
#| fig-cap: "Coverage of the 95% bootstrap CIs of the limits of agreement, 40 patients × 8 measurements, with ±1.96 Monte Carlo SE. Dotted: idea 2 for the observation bootstrap. Dashed: 95%."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
observation_theory <- tibble(icc = seq(0, 0.8, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(coverage = observation_bootstrap_coverage(icc, n_patients = 40, n_per_patient = 8, V = V))

loa_coverage |>
  filter(block == "ICC") |>
  ggplot(aes(icc, coverage, color = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = observation_theory, aes(icc, coverage), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            color = "grey30", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(position = position_dodge(width = 0.04), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = coverage - z * mcse_coverage, ymax = coverage + z * mcse_coverage),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.04)) +
  facet_wrap(~ limit, labeller = as_labeller(c(lower = "Lower LoA", upper = "Upper LoA"))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = ci_method_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "Resampling patients, not measurements, fixes the LoA CIs",
       x = "ICC", y = "Coverage of the 95% CI") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")
```

```{r}
#| label: study1-loa-table
loa_coverage |>
  arrange(block != "ICC", icc, n_per_patient, method) |>
  select(scenario, method, limit, coverage, width) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = limit, values_from = c(coverage, width)) |>
  select(scenario, method, coverage_lower, width_lower, coverage_upper, width_upper) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "scenario") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = starts_with("coverage"), decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_number(columns = starts_with("width"), decimals = 2) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Lower LoA", columns = ends_with("lower")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Upper LoA", columns = ends_with("upper")) |>
  tab_header(title = "95% bootstrap CIs of the limits of agreement", subtitle = "Width in L/min") |>
  cols_label(method = "", coverage_lower = "Coverage", width_lower = "Width",
             coverage_upper = "Coverage", width_upper = "Width")
```

The observation bootstrap follows idea 2, 1 to 3 points below it, the same kind of shortfall that the percentile interval already has at ICC = 0.
The resampling unit matters much more than the estimator: with a patient bootstrap, the classical and the additive limits have almost the same coverage.
Still, both patient bootstrap intervals stay a few points below 95% at every ICC, and more so with fewer patients (compare 20, 40 and 80 patients in the table).
The patients are the independent units, and with few of them the percentile bootstrap is too narrow.

**Predictive coverage.** For a new patient, a future difference is $D \sim N(\beta_0, V)$, so the share of future differences between the estimated limits is

$$
p_b = \Phi\left(\frac{\hat U_b - \beta_0}{\sqrt V}\right) - \Phi\left(\frac{\hat L_b - \beta_0}{\sqrt V}\right).
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-predictive-study1
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the predictive coverage over the simulated datasets, 40 patients × 8 measurements. Diamond: mean. Dashed: 95%."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
# Share of N(mean, sd^2) between lower and upper
predictive_coverage <- function(lower, upper, mean, sd) {
  pnorm((upper - mean) / sd) - pnorm((lower - mean) / sd)
}

predictive_1 <- study1 |>
  filter(block == "ICC") |>
  mutate(Classical = predictive_coverage(classical_lower_loa, classical_upper_loa, true_bias, sd_total),
         `Additive model` = predictive_coverage(additive_lower_loa, additive_upper_loa, true_bias, sd_total)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Classical, `Additive model`), names_to = "method", values_to = "coverage") |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = c("Classical", "Additive model")))

ggplot(predictive_1, aes(factor(icc), coverage, fill = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.size = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 2,
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = method_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "The estimated limits still contain about 95% of future differences",
       x = "ICC", y = "Predictive coverage") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

As idea 1 says, clustering hardly changes the limits themselves, only their uncertainty.
The mean predictive coverage is slightly below 95% for both methods, because the limits are estimated. Near the true limits, coverage is a concave function of each limit, so random error in $\hat L$ and $\hat U$ loses more coverage than it gains.

### D. Study 2 in full {#sec-appendix-d}

The reference $X$ comes from `simulate_study()`, log-normal around 5 L/min, with about 98% of the values between 2.5 and 10 L/min.
Both scenarios have a geometric mean ratio of 1.05 and a log-scale ICC of 0.338, for 40 patients with 8 measurements each. Only the total SD $\sigma$ of $\log(Y/X)$ changes.

**What the additive model converges to.**

```{r}
#| label: study2-theory-check
# Idea 3: the limits of the additive model, predicted vs mean over the simulated datasets
simulated_2 <- study2 |>
  summarize(mu_d = mean(additive_bias),
            c_d = mean(additive_sd_patient^2),
            v_d = mean(additive_sd_patient^2 + additive_sd_residual^2),
            lower_star = mean(additive_lower_loa),
            upper_star = mean(additive_upper_loa),
            .by = sd_log_total) |>
  left_join(select(theory_2, scenario, sd_log_total), by = "sd_log_total")

bind_rows(Predicted = select(theory_2, scenario, mu_d, c_d, v_d, lower_star, upper_star),
          `Simulated mean` = select(simulated_2, scenario, mu_d, c_d, v_d, lower_star, upper_star),
          .id = "source") |>
  arrange(desc(scenario), source) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "scenario") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(mu_d, c_d, v_d, lower_star, upper_star), decimals = 3) |>
  tab_header(title = "The additive model converges to the predicted constant limits",
             subtitle = "Idea 3. Bias and limits in L/min, variances in (L/min)².") |>
  cols_label(source = "", mu_d = "Bias", c_d = "Variance between patients",
             v_d = "Total variance", lower_star = "Lower LoA", upper_star = "Upper LoA")
```

**Confidence intervals for the limits of agreement.** The additive model has no single true value to compare its constant limits with, so its CIs are compared with the true limits at low, typical and high CO.

```{r}
#| label: study2-loa-ci
study2 |>
  select(scenario, replicate, true_bias, sd_log_total, ends_with(c("_ci_low", "_ci_high"))) |>
  pivot_longer(ends_with(c("_ci_low", "_ci_high")),
               names_to = c("method", "limit", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "(additive|multiplicative)_(lower|upper)_loa_ci_(low|high)") |>
  cross_join(tibble(co = c(3, 5, 8))) |>
  mutate(
    # CI in L/min at this CO. The multiplicative CI is for log(Y/X).
    low = if_else(method == "multiplicative", co * (exp(low) - 1), low),
    high = if_else(method == "multiplicative", co * (exp(high) - 1), high),
    true_log_loa = if_else(limit == "lower", true_bias - z * sd_log_total, true_bias + z * sd_log_total),
    truth = co * (exp(true_log_loa) - 1),
    covered = low <= truth & truth <= high,
    method = factor(method, levels = c("additive", "multiplicative"),
                    labels = c("Additive model", "Multiplicative model"))
  ) |>
  summarize(coverage = mean(covered), .by = c(scenario, method, limit, co)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(limit, co), values_from = coverage) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "scenario") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = -c(scenario, method), decimals = 1) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Lower LoA", columns = starts_with("lower")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Upper LoA", columns = starts_with("upper")) |>
  tab_header(title = "Coverage of the 95% CIs of the limits of agreement",
             subtitle = "Against the true limits in L/min at a reference CO of 3, 5 and 8 L/min") |>
  cols_label(method = "", lower_3 = "CO 3", lower_5 = "CO 5", lower_8 = "CO 8",
             upper_3 = "CO 3", upper_5 = "CO 5", upper_8 = "CO 8")
```

The CIs of the multiplicative model have the same coverage at every CO, because $x(e^{t} - 1)$ is increasing in $t$. It is a little below 95%, for the same reason as the patient bootstrap in Study 1.
As idea 3 says, the CIs of the additive model can only be right near the CO where its constant limits cross the true lines.
At 5 L/min, close to $x_U$ = `r sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", theory_2$x_upper[1], theory_2$x_upper[2])` L/min (mild and marked), the upper limit is covered in most datasets.
The lower limit crosses its true line at a higher CO, $x_L$ = `r sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", theory_2$x_lower[1], theory_2$x_lower[2])` L/min, so it is missed at all three CO in the table.

  gt(groupname_col = "scenario") |>
